semantic_correction.stem: A hospital is implementing an Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health (AIM) patient safety bundle for obstetric hemorrhage. Which implementation approach best reflects the purpose of the bundle?

options.A: Use evidence-informed bundle practices, adapt implementation to local resources, standardize the facility process, and preserve individualized clinical judgment.
options.B: Adopt the published bundle as the facility’s fixed order set, keeping the national wording and workflow unchanged so implementation is consistent across settings.
options.C: Select the bundle elements that fit the current workflow first and postpone the remaining system changes until outcome data show that additional steps are needed.
options.D: Use completion of the bundle checklist as the main guide for each hemorrhage event, with individualized treatment decisions made after the checklist is finished.

semantic_correction.rationale: The current Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health patient-safety-bundle guidance describes bundles as collections of evidence-informed best practices developed by multidisciplinary experts to improve care processes and outcomes for clinically specific maternal conditions. AIM states that bundles contain actionable steps that can be adapted to different facilities and resource levels and that bundle guidance is not meant to be prescriptive. The current Obstetric Hemorrhage bundle likewise states that its actionable steps can be adapted to facility and resource level. Its Element Implementation Details specify a standardized, facility-wide, stage-based obstetric hemorrhage emergency management plan and identify multidisciplinary review and updates to standard policies and procedures as part of systems learning. Therefore A best captures the intended implementation model: evidence-informed practices adapted to local capabilities, standardized into the facility's care process, while bedside assessment and patient-specific treatment remain individualized. B wrongly converts adaptable guidance into an unchanged national order set. C can resemble operational phasing, but it makes completion of coordinated system changes contingent on later outcome failure rather than implementing the evidence-informed safety framework with appropriate local adaptation. D incorrectly allows checklist completion to displace ongoing clinical assessment and individualized treatment decisions.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Implement maternal patient safety bundles as evidence-informed, standardized quality-improvement frameworks that are adapted to local resources while preserving individualized clinical assessment and treatment.

semantic_correction.source_locator: AIM Patient Safety Bundles — PSBs are collections of evidence-informed best practices developed by multidisciplinary experts; goal is improvement of care processes and outcomes; actionable steps can be adapted to different facilities/resource levels; bundle guidance is not meant to be prescriptive. AIM Obstetric Hemorrhage webpage — bundle provides actionable steps adaptable to a variety of facilities and resource levels. Obstetric Hemorrhage Element Implementation Details, Readiness (PDF p.2 / pageno 1): implement a standardized, facility-wide, stage-based emergency management plan; Levels of Maternal Care are based on known facility level/resources. Reporting and Systems Learning (PDF p.6 / pageno 5): multidisciplinary review evaluates alignment with standard policies/procedures and appropriate updates to those policies/procedures.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: AIM patient safety bundles are evidence-informed quality-improvement frameworks with actionable practices that can be adapted to local resources, standardized in facility processes, and used without replacing patient-specific assessment or clinical judgment.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the AIM-bundle implementation construct, removed the old must/only and length cues, rebuilt all alternatives as realistic implementation strategies of equal length, and grounded local adaptation plus facility standardization in current AIM resources without treating a bundle as a substitute for individualized clinical judgment.

scope_exclusions.exclusive_treatment: The item does not claim the bundle dictates one exclusive clinical treatment course; current AIM guidance explicitly describes bundle guidance as non-prescriptive.
scope_exclusions.optional_core_elements: Local adaptation concerns implementation to resources and setting; it is not framed as permission to arbitrarily discard core safety processes whenever they are inconvenient.
scope_exclusions.order_set: A patient safety bundle is not treated as a national medication order set or a replacement for provider orders and facility-specific protocols.
scope_exclusions.clinical_judgment: Standardized system processes support but do not replace ongoing assessment, escalation, shared decision-making, contraindication review, or individualized treatment.
scope_exclusions.resource_level: Facilities may adapt implementation to their available resources and Level of Maternal Care while establishing referral/escalation pathways when resources are limited.
scope_exclusions.specific_hemorrhage_treatment: The item tests implementation governance rather than the choice of uterotonics, tranexamic acid, transfusion, tamponade, embolization, or surgery.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for ‘AIM patient safety bundle evidence informed adapt local resources standardized facility clinical judgment obstetric hemorrhage’ returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank scan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It integrates AIM's evidence-informed, adaptable, non-prescriptive framework with the bundle's facility-wide standardization and continued patient-specific judgment.
option_audit.B: Plausible because standardization is important, but AIM permits adaptation to facility resources and does not define the bundle as an unchanged national order set.
option_audit.C: Plausible because implementation can be phased operationally, but making completion of coordinated system changes depend on later outcome failure misrepresents an evidence-informed safety framework.
option_audit.D: Plausible because checklists and standardized plans improve reliability, but they support rather than replace bedside assessment and individualized treatment.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A alone combines evidence-informed practice, local adaptation, facility standardization, and preserved clinical judgment. B is too rigid across settings, C improperly conditions coordinated system implementation on later outcome failure, and D lets the checklist supersede individualized care.

cueing_check.note: All four alternatives are parallel implementation strategies with essentially identical length; the key is tied for shortest and no all/only/must/always/never/every cue is used.
